findings.reason: The protected implementation is the canonical concise interview solution: num.bit_length() identifies exactly the significant width, (1 << width) - 1 creates the bounded all-ones mask, and XOR performs the requested flips. The two executable lines are clear, conventional, correctly named, and contain no unnecessary state or obscure trick, so no candidate is justified.

Metadata consistently identifies public LeetCode problem 476, its Python integer method, and its runnable solve(num) adapter. The positive-input contract guarantees a nonzero significant width, and the mask excludes implicit leading zeroes while flipping every bit from the highest set bit through the least significant bit.

The protected app source and immutable native source bound to verified submission 2064984986 are algorithmically identical: both compute the same bit-length-derived mask and return num XOR mask. Their only structural difference is the native Solution.findComplement wrapper.

The legal 4-bit, 16-bit, and 31-bit power-of-two workloads span more than 7x in significant width and exercise leading-one removal plus lower-zero inversion. The exact current source passed all 10 opaque correctness executions and all three performance tiers at 1.02x the calibrated reference runtime. A correct implementation that rebuilt each successive bit mask from bit zero passed every opaque output but failed only performance at 6.41x the reference runtime.

For significant width b = O(log num), the algorithm requires at most O(b) conceptual bit work and O(1) auxiliary scalar state. Under the source's strict 31-bit domain, Python's width, shift, subtraction, and XOR operations are constant bounded; the manifest's O(log num) time and O(1) space claims are therefore conservative and sound.

The current-targeted Approach exactly derives the significant-bit mask, explains XOR's bit-flip behavior, proves that no leading position is introduced, defines the width variable used by its complexity bound, and covers one, powers of two, all-ones inputs, and excluded leading zeroes.

The hash-bound modular Reference was checked directly against the live public statement. It preserves the binary flip definition, the illustrative 5 -> 101 -> 010 -> 2 sequence, both examples and explanations in order, the no-leading-zero detail, the strict 2^31 bound, the trailing note equating the task with frontend ID 1009, and the absence of visuals or tables.
